accepted.question_text: Let F be a distribution on R or R^d that is n-completely mixable, meaning there exist random variables X1, ..., Xn all having distribution F and satisfying X1 + ··· + Xn = nµ for some center µ. Must that center be unique? Equivalently, if µ and ν are distinct real numbers, is it impossible for the same distribution to belong to both M_n(µ) and M_n(ν)?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 1. Is the center of mixability always unique for a distribution on R (or R d )? In other words, for µ, ν ∈ R, µ 6= ν, is it true that Mn(µ) ∩ Mn(ν) = ∅?

accepted.question_text: Can the main complete-mixability and joint-mixability theorems be proved by a generic probabilistic or analytic method, instead of the current long combinatorial and discretization arguments? In particular, is there a general proof strategy that avoids mathematical induction on discretized approximations and makes the dependence structure of the resulting joint mix transparent?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 2. Is there a generic (probabilistic, analytic) proof of the main results in complete and joint mixability?
The proofs for the above-mentioned results are typically very long and technical, and more importantly the details of the dependence structure for a joint mix are always unclear.

accepted.question_text: Suppose X is a joint mix taking values in Z_+^n with fixed joint center N, so that X can be decomposed as X = Σ_{k=1}^N X_k where each X_k is a binary multinomial random vector. Can this decomposition be used in a non-trivial way to characterize additional classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions, and if so, how?

evidence.quote: Theorem 3. Suppose that X takes values in Z+. X is a joint mix with joint center N ∈ Z+ if and only if it has the following representation X = ∑Nk=1 Xk, where Xk, k = 1, . . . , N are binary multinomial random vectors.
Open Problem 3. Is Theorem 3 helpful (and how) in characterizing more classes of CM and JM distributions?

accepted.question_text: Let F be a distribution with mean µ. Assume that for every law-determined norm ||·|| and every real threshold t, the inequalities ||(X − t)+|| ≤ (n − 1)||(X − s)−|| and ||(X − t)−|| ≤ (n − 1)||(X − s)+|| hold for X ∼ F and s = (nµ − t)/(n − 1). Under what additional assumptions, such as smoothness conditions, are these inequalities sufficient to conclude that F is n-completely mixable?

evidence.quote: Theorem 5. Suppose that F is n-CM with center µ, X ∼ F and || · || is any law-determined norm. Then we have that ||(X − t)+|| 6 (n − 1)||(X − s)−|| and ||(X − t)−|| 6 (n − 1)||(X − s)+||, for all t ∈ R and s = (nµ − t)/(n − 1).

Open Problem 4. Suppose that F has mean µ, and (14) holds for all law-determined norms || · || and all t ∈ R. (With what extra conditions, possibly some smoothness conditions) is it sufficient for F to be n-CM?

accepted.question_text: If C is a convex subset of R^d and F is the uniform distribution on C, must F be n-completely mixable for every n ≥ d + 1? Equivalently, is every uniform distribution on a convex set in R^d already (d + 1)-completely mixable?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 5. Is a uniform distribution on a convex set C ⊂ R d necessarily n-CM for all n > d + 1?
Obviously, the above conjecture is equivalent to say that a uniform distribution on a convex set C ⊂ R d is (d + 1)-CM.

accepted.question_text: Let F be a distribution on R^d with d > 1. Suppose that for every essential subspace of R^d, the projection of F onto that subspace is n-completely mixable. Under what additional conditions does that imply that F itself is n-completely mixable on R^d?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 6. Suppose that F is a distribution on R d , d > 1, and the projection of F to any essential subspace of R d is n-CM. (With what extra conditions) is it sufficient for F to be n-CM on R d ?

accepted.question_text: Does every absolutely continuous distribution supported on a bounded interval become n-completely mixable once n is large enough? In other words, can the known asymptotic complete-mixability results be extended beyond densities that are bounded away from zero?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 7. Are all absolutely continuous distributions on a bounded interval n-CM for large enough n?

As a consequence, any continuous distribution with a density bounded away from zero is n-CM for n sufficiently large. It is left open to answer whether this condition of a density bounded away from zero can be removed.

accepted.question_text: Suppose a distribution F is known to be n-completely mixable by an available sufficient condition. Can one write down an explicit copula for an n-complete mix with margins F, or more generally for a joint mix with the given margins?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 8. Suppose that F satisfies one of the sufficient conditions (for instance, (b) in Section 2.2) and hence is n-CM. What is a possible copula of a n-complete mix with margins F (or a joint mix with given margins)?

accepted.question_text: Suppose a distribution F is known to be n-completely mixable by an available sufficient condition. Is there an effective way to simulate samples from an n-complete mix with margins F?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 9. Suppose that F satisfies one of the sufficient conditions (for instance, (b) in Section 2.2) and hence is n-CM. Could we simulate sample from a n-complete mix with margins F?

accepted.question_text: For a unimodal distribution supported on a bounded interval, what additional conditions guarantee n-complete mixability? This asks for hypotheses beyond unimodality alone, since the mean condition by itself is known not to be sufficient in general.

evidence.quote: Open Problem 10. Under what extra conditions a unimodal distribution on a bounded interval is n-CM?
[34] gave counter-examples where the mean condition (15) is not sufficient for the complete mixability of a distribution with a unimodal density on a bounded interval.

accepted.question_text: Given marginal distributions F1, ..., Fn and the aggregation set D_n = {X1 + ··· + Xn : Xi ∼ Fi for i = 1, ..., n}, what are necessary and sufficient conditions for D_n to contain an element S0 that is smallest with respect to convex order, meaning S0 ≺cx S for every S in D_n?

evidence.quote: For some univariate distributions F1, . . . , Fn, define the aggregation set Dn = {X1 + · · · + Xn : Xi ∈ X , Xi ∼ Fi , i = 1, . . . , n} ⊂ X .
Open Problem 11. What are necessary and sufficient conditions for Dn to contain a smallest element with respect to convex order?

accepted.question_text: Given marginal distributions F1, ..., Fn, characterize the aggregation set D_n by deciding which target distributions G can occur as the law of some sum S = X1 + ··· + Xn with Xi ∼ Fi. Equivalently, for a specified distribution G, determine whether there exists S ∈ D_n such that S has distribution G.

evidence.quote: Open Problem 12. How can one characterize Dn (maybe for some simple marginal distributions)? That is, for a given distribution G, determine whether S ∈ Dn for some S ∼ G.

accepted.question_text: Develop algorithms that determine whether specified distributions are jointly mixable, or that solve the minimax assignment problem of arranging workers so as to minimize the maximum row sum in the production model. In particular, under what conditions do the swapping algorithms proposed for this purpose converge?

evidence.quote: 1. Algorithms to determine whether some distributions are jointly mixable, or solving question (1) in Section 1: see for instance [28, 12, 34, 19]. The conditions under which the swapping algorithms in [28] converges are still unclear.
In particular, [19] showed that question (i) in Section 1.2 is NP-complete even in the case when all ai,j ∈ Z.

accepted.question_text: Extend mixability to higher-dimensional marginal constraints: when some fixed bivariate or higher-dimensional marginal distributions are prescribed, determine whether a joint mix exists and develop numerical algorithms to decide existence or construct one.

evidence.quote: 2. Mixability under higher-dimensional constraints: for fixed bivariate or higher-dimensional marginal distributions, determine whether a joint mix exists and develop algorithms for numerical determination.

accepted.question_text: Generalize the definition of mixability by replacing the summation X1 + ··· + Xn with other multivariate functions, and determine what corresponding notions of complete or joint mixability are mathematically useful and how they can be characterized.

evidence.quote: 3. Other multivariate functions replacing the summation of random variables in the definition of mixability; see [4].

accepted.question_text: How does the algebraic structure of the underlying semigroup G affect complete and joint mixability defined on G? In particular, which properties of G help or obstruct the existence, uniqueness, or characterization of mixes?

evidence.quote: 4. The influence of the algebraic structure of a semigroup G on complete and joint mixability defined on G.
